text:
marta: Heads up — us-west-2c is flapping on GPU provisioning. Noticed a surge of node cordons today, kube-scheduler can't place pods. Root cause looks like local NVMe scrub backlog and write stalls on ephemeral volumes.

devon: Seen the same. Alerting dashboard shows scrub_worker queue depth skyrocketed around 06:12 PDT. I/O latencies > 200ms on /dev/nvme0n1.

marta: Attach from node-uw2c-044 logs:
```
Jun 05 06:14:03 node-uw2c-044 nvme-scrubber[1123]: scrub_task: read error sector 0x1f4b2
Jun 05 06:14:04 node-uw2c-044 kernel: blk_update_request: I/O error, dev nvme0n1, sector 12921344
Jun 05 06:15:10 node-uw2c-044 kubelet[823]: Evicting pods: local disk pressure
```

zane: Oof. Are these ephemeral-only instances? Looks like preemptible pool with older controller firmware.

lucy: Confirmed: these are spot-dedicated-gpu nodes (type g4x-ephemeral). Firmware levels show 1.12 on most; our recommended is 1.15+.

sam: Quick mitigation: can we pause the scrubber jobs and drain the worst nodes? We'll lose some cleanup but prevent new evictions.

infra-bot: (automated) 2051236805 — created incident INC-uw2c-scrub-01, priority P2. Notifying oncall.

oncall-bot: @oncall paging: please triage INC-uw2c-scrub-01 — high gpu provisioning impact.

devon: Action plan proposal: 1) Disable aggressive scrub rate on affected hosts (set rate=0.2) 2) Move GPU scheduling to healthy AZs only for next 2 hours 3) Roll nodes with firmware update + NVMe reformat in maintenance window.

marta: Agree. Also add a temporary scheduler predicate: avoid nodes with nvme_lat_95 > 50ms. I'll open a k8s feature-flag.

zane: On the firmware front, rolling update isn't instant. If we drain too many GPUs from us-west-2c we might exhaust capacity and hit backlog for customers with dedicated slots. Cost/impact: moving jobs to us-west-2b will increase latency for a subset and could consume reserved capacity.

lucy: We should also throttle our ephemeral-cleaner concurrency. Current default is 16 workers per node; drop to 4 to reduce IOPS pressure.

sam: I'm running a quick probe script to find nodes with the highest scrub backlog:
```
for n in $(kubectl get nodes -l pool=gpu -o name); do
  ssh $n 'cat /var/log/nvme-scrub/metrics.log | tail -n1'
done
```
Got a top list: node-uw2c-044, -051, -063 are worst.

marta: Ok. Devon, can you coordinate a quick cordon+drain of those three and flip the scheduler avoidance? I'll push a patch to the daemonset to reduce cleaner workers.

devon: On it. Cordon/drain in 2m. Also enabled patch to kube-scheduler configmap to add the nvme predicate.

infra-bot: (automated) 2051236890 — node-uw2c-044 cordoned by devon.

zane: After draining two nodes, we still saw a spike in eviction metrics because the scrub backlog spread to neighboring nodes due to sudden extra cleanup. We need rate limit + backoff.

lucy: I've pushed cleaner change with concurrency=4 and added exponential backoff for errors. Updated image tag: infra/ephemeral-cleaner:v1.3.2.

sam: Monitoring now. Early signs: avg NVMe IOPS down ~35% on drained nodes, lat_p95 falling from 220ms -> 85ms. Scheduler can place small pods again.

marta: Good. Longer term: prioritize firmware rollout for preemptible pool, add a metric export for scrub queue depth, and schedule weekly low-intensity scrub windows to avoid peak allocation times.

zane: Also add a capacity buffer policy: reserve 10% GPU headroom in each AZ so a single AZ NVMe degradation doesn't block provisioning globally. That will cost more but improves availability.

lucy: I'll draft the RFC for scrub heuristics + scheduler predicate change.

marta: For the incident: mark as mitigated for now, keep monitoring for 3h, and follow up with post-incident notes. Thanks all. :thumbsup:
